idiom_name: QML documents as the presentational half; a QObject controller with Q_PROPERTY / Q_INVOKABLE as the supply half
implementation_notes: Qt's documented guidance is to write the user interface in QML and push references to C++ types into it rather than manipulating QML objects from C++: the QObject-derived controller exposes data as Q_PROPERTY with a NOTIFY signal and behaviour as Q_INVOKABLE methods, while the QML document renders those properties and emits signals back - it holds no data, no network client and no source of truth. What replaces the classic container component is the property/signal pair (with required properties set on the root object, not context properties), and Qt's own model/view/delegate split replaces it again for large item sets, where QAbstractItemModel carries the data and the view renders from it. Prefer the widgets variant when the application is already a widgets application.
pitfalls: Walking into loaded QML objects from C++ (findChild, setProperty on item names) re-couples the supply half to markup object names and breaks the separation the controller exists to create.
A property exposed without a NOTIFY signal gives QML no change notification, so the view silently keeps stale values.
QML documents can call any registered type they can reach: if a document imports the network client directly, the presentational half is no longer presentational.

variants.name: Qt Widgets: QWidget page as supply half, passive child widgets
variants.idiom_name: QWidget/QLayout page owning the data; children configured through setters and signals
variants.implementation_notes: In the widgets stack the supply half is a QWidget subclass (or a page inside a QMainWindow) that owns the model and wires the children with signals and slots; the child widgets are passive - they display what they are set to and emit signals, and never reach for the data themselves. For large item sets Qt's model/view classes extend the same idea: a QAbstractItemModel supplies the data and a QStyledItemDelegate paints it, so the widget holds no copy. Choose this variant when the application is already a widgets application or needs imperative control over the view hierarchy; QML is the better fit for designer-authored, declarative interfaces.
pitfalls: Child widgets that keep their own copy of the model data drift out of sync; set them from the supply half and treat them as output devices.
Children held as bare pointers without a parent leak or dangle; parent them to the owning widget or hold them in owning smart pointers.
Running blocking work in a slot freezes the GUI thread - the supply half should delegate to a worker and marshal the result back.
